ABSTRACT: Selectivity control is a very challenging topic in catalytic
oxidations of alcohols using oxygen as an oxidant. Of particular interest
is the catalytic aerobic lactonization of diols; due to the selectivity issue
referring to the two hydroxy groups, the reaction afforded a mixture of
isomeric products. Herein, we report an efficient catalytic recipe of
easily available earth-abundant metal catalysts
\mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } 9 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }
and
\mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 }
together with TEMPO for the highly selective aerobic oxidative
lactonization of 1,6-diols, affording a variety of ε-caprolactones. The reaction was conducted under mild conditions with an O2
balloon or under ambient air enjoying high chemo- and regioselectivity for the oxidative lactonization of non-symmetric diols by the
subtle recognition of the steric environment of the two hydroxy groups. Furthermore, reduction and selective aerobic oxidative
lactonization constitute a formal carbonyl walking over the ε-caprolactones. Mechanistic experiments reveal a process with a
hemiacetal as the intermediate. This protocol unlocks an efficient pathway to derive monomers for polycaprolactones.
KEYWORDS: caprolactone, diols, iron catalysis, aerobic oxidative lactonization, polycaprolactone

Functionalized PCLs have been synthesized by ring-opening
polymerization of corresponding caprolactone monomers.3
Given that the reported caprolactone monomers feature 2- and
4-substituted functional groups,10,11 we attempted to make full
use of the current approach for new caprolactones with
untapped potential. Fortunately, 5-substituted caprolactone 2D
could be obtained through the oxidative lactonization of diol
1D with an excellent selectivity (Scheme 4). The deprotection
of 2D was successfully achieved to form the non-symmetric
caprolactone 8 with a free hydroxy group. Further function-
alization of 8 afforded compound carboxylate 9 with 2-
bromoisobutyryl bromide, benzyl ether 10 with benzyl
bromide, and carboxylate 11 with pivalic anhydride,
respectively. It is worth noting that the symmetric homologue
of 2D (compound

and the isomers of 9−11

\hat { \mathbf { 9 ^ { \prime } } } - \mathbf { 1 1 ^ { \prime } } ) ^ { 5 1 - 5 3 }
have been applied as the building
blocks of PCL. We expect that our strategy may pave the way
